newsitem.title: USA: Mobil says in talks to link refining units.
newsitem.headline: Mobil says in talks to link refining units.

text.p: Mobil Corp. said Monday it was looking for a partner to boost profits at the gasoline pump, becoming the latest big oil company to weigh a linkup to bolster its refining and marketing operations.

"We are continually looking to improve marketing and refining in the U.S. We have had and continue to have discussions with several, and I emphasise the word 'several,' companies," said Mobil spokesman Christopher Springham.
"None has reached the stage where it is possible to reach any conclusions," he said.
Springham declined to comment on a report that Fairfax, Va.-based company Mobil was discussing a merger of those businesses with Amoco Corp.

The report was first published in the business section of the Sunday Telegraph, a London newspaper, which quoted unidentified sources that said Mobil was "deep in talks" with Chicago-based Amoco to merge their refining and marketing operations in the United States and overseas.
The newspaper article speculated the deal would involve around $20 billion of assets. Amoco officials were not immediately available for comment.
Wall Street welcomed such a possible linkup. Mobil stock jumped $2.625 to $136.75 and Amoco gained $2.75 to $87.50 on the New York Stock Exchange.

Amoco and Mobil have big refineries in the South and Midwest. Mobil also has plants on the East and West Coasts and in Louisiana, while Amoco has large Texas and Indiana refineries and a smattering of plants from Virginia to Utah.
Faced with weak refining profits, oil producers have little choice but to merge downstream operations, analysts said.
"There appears to be a realisation that these companies are not going to benefit substantially from margin improvements," said Philip Tendler at Schroder Wertheim.
Mobil Chairman Lucio Noto told reporters at the company's annual meeting recently that improving returns in refining operations was a key concern.
Amoco has said it is seeking a partner for its downstream assets, and analysts say Atlantic Richfield Co. and Sun Co. are looking to hook up with a U.S. partner.

A marriage of Amoco and Mobil's operations would link the No. 3 and No. 5 U.S. refiners with combined capacity to process nearly 2 million barrels a day of crude oil, according to the Oil & Gas Journal, an industry magazine.
Already, some of the biggest names in the industry have said they will form joint ventures.

Last year, Texaco Inc. and Shell Oil Co. agreed to merge their U.S. interests, including Texaco's joint venture with Saudi Aramco, Star Enterprises. Also, Mobil has agreed to link its European refining and marketing assets in Europe with those of British Petroleum Co. Plc.
In the United States, nine out of the top 25 refiners have been involved in mergers, acquisitions or "alliances" in the last year and industry officials expect more deals.
Only last week, Marathon Oil Co. and Ashland Inc. announced a linkup of their U.S. refining and marketing businesses in a 62/38 percent split.
U.S. refining profit margins continue to drop, averaging $4.85 a barrel recently compared with $6.25 a year ago. Oil companies are hoping mergers will help reverse the decline.
"The problem is that there is still very little pricing power in this industry and that when there are cost reductions, they are passed on to the consumer," said Schroder's Tendler.
"Amoco and Mobil looks like a deal that would make sense, but there is a lot of work to do on valuing assets and clearing any antitrust objections," said Asit Sen, an analyst for Oppenheimer & Co.
